title: Escalation Playbook v2 — Support Training: Agenda + Exercises (w/ Answer Key)
content:
Slide 1 — Title
Escalation Playbook v2
Support Training: Severity + SLAs + Escalation Flow
Scenario-based exercises (with answer key)
Owner: Dev Patel (Program Lead)
Co-facilitators: Owen Phillips (Support Eng), Rafael Mendes (SRE), Priya Shah (Known Issues)

Slide 2 — Why we’re doing this
What changed since v1:
- Volume is up across Hosted + Dedicated + Private; inconsistencies in triage have become customer-visible.
- Repeated escalations are missing the same info (request IDs, model/version, region, timestamps, streaming mode).
- SLA expectations weren’t aligned (Support ↔ SRE ↔ Customer), especially after-hours.
- We now have a curated Known Issues & Workarounds set that Support can use during triage.

Success targets (Mar–Apr 2026):
- Reduce time-to-resolution for top 5 escalation drivers.
- Reduce “ping-pong” between Support and Eng due to incomplete intake.
- Increase ticket deflection via Known Issues pages and consistent customer guidance.

Slide 3 — Training agenda (75 minutes)
0) Pre-reads (before session, 10 min)
1) Severity & what constitutes an escalation (15 min)
2) SLA expectations by tier + comms cadence (10 min)
3) Escalation flow + required fields (10 min)
4) Exercises (25 min)
5) Q&A + rollout checklist (5 min)

Optional: deep dive on “incident vs escalation” (10 min add-on)

Slide 4 — Pre-reads / references (send in calendar invite)
- Confluence: Escalation Playbook v2 Overview
- Confluence: Severity Matrix & Triage Criteria
- Confluence: Support + Eng SLAs by Tier
- Confluence: Escalation Paths & Ownership Map
- Confluence: Known Issues Index

Slide 5 — Guiding principles (how we want triage to feel)
- Fast, consistent classification. Don’t spend 45 minutes debating P1 vs P2.
- “Escalation” is a decision with consequences (paging + context switching). Use triggers.
- The first escalation message must be actionable. If it’s missing required data, it isn’t ready.
- Prefer safe mitigations and validated workarounds over speculative advice.
- Protect customer-identifying data for Private/enterprise accounts (restricted handling).

Slide 6 — Definitions (terms used in v2)
- Customer-facing severity: P0–P4 (what the customer experiences / impact)
- Internal incident severity: Sev0–Sev3 (SRE incident process)
- “Escalation”: Support requests Eng/SRE engagement beyond normal async consult.
- “Incident”: coordinated SRE-led response, usually multi-customer or infrastructure-level risk.

Rule of thumb:
- Not every escalation is an incident.
- Some incidents start from a single enterprise ticket if blast radius is unknown + signals are concerning.

Slide 7 — Severity matrix (quick reference)
P0 (Critical): Production is down OR severe degradation with no workaround
Examples:
- Hosted: sustained 5xx/timeouts across a region/model affecting many requests
- Dedicated: near-zero throughput or persistent latency > SLA with business-critical impact
- Private: auth/SSO outage preventing all users from accessing Console/API
Expected: immediate escalation; likely incident depending on scope

P1 (High): Major feature impaired or significant degradation; workaround may exist but is risky/limited
Examples:
- Intermittent streaming disconnects impacting a critical workflow
- Elevated 429s due to misconfig or limit regression impacting launch
Expected: escalation if triggers hit; proactive comms cadence

P2 (Medium): Partial impact; workaround exists and is acceptable
Examples:
- One model/version impacted, customer can pin rollback or switch model
- Dedicated latency spikes at peak with mitigation knobs available

P3 (Low): Minor impact or question; no urgent risk
Examples:
- SDK integration help; one-off error with low frequency

P4 (Info): How-to, billing, feature request

Slide 8 — Escalation triggers (don’t “feel” your way into paging)
Escalate to SRE/Oncall if any of the following are true:
- Suspected platform regression or outage (5xx/timeout spike signals, multi-customer risk)
- Customer is enterprise/private/dedicated AND impact is P0/P1
- There is a credible security/authentication break (SSO login failures, token validation issues)
- Dedicated capacity shortfall: sustained queueing / throughput collapse without customer-side explanation
- You cannot provide a validated workaround within the next update window

Escalate to Runtime/Platform Eng (non-page) if:
- Reproducible bug with request IDs and consistent steps
- Model-specific behavior regression tied to pinned version

Do NOT escalate (yet) if:
- Missing required fields (ask customer first or use logs/internal tooling)
- Known issue with validated workaround that resolves impact (document + monitor)

Slide 9 — “Incident vs Escalation” decision aid
Declare incident (or ask SRE to declare) when:
- Multi-customer signal is likely OR blast radius unknown and risk is high
- Core shared component impacted: api-gateway, routing, scheduler, serving runtime, auth/rbac, quota enforcement
- We need coordinated comms (status page + consistent updates)

Keep as support escalation when:
- Single customer configuration issue (quota setting, SDK retry policy, Private IdP mismatch)
- Dedicated tuning/sizing issue with clear ownership and no broader risk

Reference: Confluence — Support Escalation Comms Alignment

Slide 10 — SLAs by customer tier (what we commit internally)
Note: Use exact numbers from Confluence SLA table during live session. This slide is a summary of expectations.

Self-serve (Hosted API):
- Faster first response during business hours; best-effort after-hours
- Escalate only when signals suggest platform issue or high-impact launch risk

Dedicated:
- Tighter response and update cadence
- Escalate earlier for sustained latency/throughput degradation

Private / Enterprise:
- Highest comms rigor; restricted handling rules apply
- Earlier engagement of Security/Private Deployments for SSO/audit-log/network issues

Slide 11 — Comms cadence (minimum viable updates)
For P0/P1 (all tiers):
- Acknowledge + “investigation started” message quickly
- Provide next update time (not “we’ll update soon”)
- If mitigation applied: explicitly state what changed and what to monitor
- If we don’t know root cause yet: say so; don’t promise an RCA timeline you can’t meet

Use templates:
- Confluence: Customer Comms Templates

Slide 12 — Escalation flow (end-to-end)
1) Intake: Support creates/updates Jira ticket with required fields
2) Triage: severity classification + confirm tier + check Known Issues index
3) Mitigation: provide validated workaround when possible
4) Escalation (if triggers hit):
   - Page SRE/Oncall or engage owning team
   - Create incident thread if incident criteria met
5) Customer updates: align with incident comms; avoid contradicting status page
6) Resolution: confirm customer recovery + close loop
7) Post-incident: attach RCA link (if applicable), document learnings, update Known Issues if recurring

Slide 13 — Required fields for escalation (non-negotiable)
If any are missing, you’re not ready to escalate (unless P0 and you’re actively collecting while escalating).

Required:
- Customer tier + deployment mode (Hosted / Dedicated / Private)
- Impact summary (what broke, how many users/requests, when started)
- Region + model name + model version/pin (if applicable)
- Request IDs / trace IDs and timestamps (with timezone)
- Error types + counts (5xx/429/timeout/streaming disconnect) and sample payload pattern (redacted)
- SDK + version, streaming vs non-streaming, timeout settings, retry policy
- What changed recently (customer-side deploy, traffic spike, IdP change, config change)
- Links: Jira key, Slack thread, dashboards/screenshots, incident thread (if any)

Reference: Confluence — Jira Ticket Template & Required Fields

Slide 14 — Ownership map (who-to-page)
Use the ownership map to route correctly:
- 429/quota/rate-limit enforcement → API gateway & quota SME (Amara Diallo / Cole Summers)
- Streaming disconnect + runtime behavior → Runtime (Mateo Alvarez / Noah Patel) + SRE if broad
- Dedicated throughput/latency spikes → SRE + Dedicated ops/runbooks (Tomáš Novák)
- Private SSO/SAML, audit logs, KMS/HSM integrations → Private Deployments (Vivek Kulkarni) + Security (Marcus Lin)

Reference: Confluence — Escalation Paths & Ownership Map

Slide 15 — Known Issues: how to use during triage
Workflow:
1) Check Known Issues index (filter by deployment mode + region + model family)
2) Confirm symptoms match and applicability tags match customer context
3) Provide “safe-to-share” workaround only (copy/paste; don’t improvise)
4) If workaround resolves: document in ticket + follow-up ask for confirmation
5) If mismatch or no workaround: escalate with full required fields

Reference pages:
- Streaming disconnects & reconnect guidance
- 429 throttling & quota misconfiguration
- Dedicated capacity latency spikes / noisy-neighbor

Slide 16 — Exercise format
We’ll do 5 scenarios.
For each scenario, answer:
A) Severity (P0–P4)
B) Escalation? (No / Eng async / Page SRE / Declare incident)
C) First customer message (2–4 sentences)
D) What required fields are missing / what do you ask for
E) Known issue page to reference (if any) + recommended safe mitigation

Facilitator: call on one person per scenario; then reveal answer key.

------------------------------------------------------------
EXERCISES (participant slides)
------------------------------------------------------------

Slide 17 — Scenario 1: Intermittent streaming disconnects (Dedicated, us-east)
Customer: Enterprise, Dedicated deployment.
Symptoms:
- Streaming responses disconnect after ~20–40 seconds; non-streaming sometimes succeeds.
- Started today after a traffic increase (2x).
- Customer provided: timestamps, region, SDK version, and 8 request IDs.
Question: classify + route.

Slide 18 — Scenario 2: 429 spike after launch (Self-serve)
Customer: Self-serve (Hosted API).
Symptoms:
- 429s started immediately after product launch.
- Customer says “we didn’t change anything.”
- No request IDs yet. They pasted a screenshot of a 429 error from the SDK.
Question: severity + do we page?

Slide 19 — Scenario 3: Dedicated latency spikes at peak (Noisy neighbor suspected)
Customer: Dedicated.
Symptoms:
- P95 latency triples between 10am–12pm local time; throughput dips.
- Customer is at 70% of committed capacity; burst enabled.
- They can temporarily reduce max_tokens to cope.
Question: escalation criteria + mitigation.

Slide 20 — Scenario 4: Private SSO/SAML failures after IdP change
Customer: Private/VPC.
Symptoms:
- “All users can’t log in” after customer changed IdP certificate.
- Admin user also locked out.
- Customer asks for “emergency bypass” within 30 minutes.
Question: severity + who-to-engage + what to communicate.

Slide 21 — Scenario 5: Elevated 5xx in eu-west on pinned model version (Hosted, enterprise)
Customer: Enterprise on Hosted API.
Symptoms:
- Elevated 5xx in eu-west for model version pinned to “v2026-02-10”.
- us-east appears healthy; customer is reluctant to fail over due to data residency concerns.
- Customer provided request IDs and a graph of 5xx rate.
Question: incident vs escalation + comms.

Slide 22 — Breakout instructions (if >10 attendees)
Split into 2 groups:
- Group A: scenarios 1–2–3
- Group B: scenarios 4–5
Each group posts answers in Slack (internal training channel) using template:
- Severity:
- Escalation decision:
- First customer update:
- Missing fields:
- Workaround / KB link:

------------------------------------------------------------
ANSWER KEY (facilitator slides)
------------------------------------------------------------

Slide 23 — Answer key: Scenario 1 (Streaming disconnects, Dedicated)
A) Severity: P1 (High)
Rationale: enterprise dedicated customer + core functionality impaired; intermittent but impacts production workflow.

B) Escalation: Engage SRE (page if ongoing and impacting many requests) + Runtime consult.
- If metrics show elevated disconnect rate across the pool or multiple tenants: ask SRE to declare incident.
- If isolated to customer traffic pattern and we have known mitigation: keep as escalation without incident.

C) First customer message (example):
“Thanks for the details — we’re investigating the streaming disconnects in us-east on your Dedicated pool now. We’re pulling logs for the request IDs you shared and checking for elevated disconnect/timeout rates on the serving tier. Next update by <time> with what we find and recommended mitigation steps.”

D) Missing fields to request (if absent):
- Client timeout settings; whether they read the stream continuously
- Network path/proxy details (if applicable)
- Concurrency level and typical prompt length / max_tokens

E) Known issue + mitigation:
- Confluence: Streaming disconnects & reconnect guidance
- Safe mitigations: ensure client implements resumable retry on disconnect; increase read timeout; consider switching to non-streaming temporarily; request-id capture for failed attempts.

Related example ticket: Jira SUP-4921

Slide 24 — Answer key: Scenario 2 (429 spike, Self-serve)
A) Severity: P2 (Medium) by default; can be P1 if it blocks a major launch with sustained impact.

B) Escalation: NO paging initially.
- Route as support-led triage with quota verification.
- Escalate to quota/rate-limit SME only if:
  - 429s occur well below documented limits OR
  - multiple customers report unexpected 429s (potential platform regression) OR
  - customer is enterprise with contractual SLA.

C) First customer message (example):
“429s indicate you’re hitting a rate limit or quota boundary. If you can share 2–3 request IDs and your approximate request rate (RPS) and concurrency, we can confirm which limit is being hit. In the meantime, please add exponential backoff with jitter and respect the Retry-After header; we’ve included a recommended configuration below.”

D) Missing fields:
- Request IDs + timestamps
- Concurrency/RPS, burst behavior
- Org/project identifiers (internal) to check quota config

E) Known issue + mitigation:
- Confluence: 429 throttling & quota misconfiguration
- Safe mitigations: exponential backoff + jitter; cap concurrency; verify org/project limits; consider Dedicated for predictable throughput.

Related example: Jira SUP-4922; SDK guidance: GitHub redwood-sdk-python/pr_519

Slide 25 — Answer key: Scenario 3 (Dedicated latency spikes, peak hours)
A) Severity: P2 (Medium) if recoverable with mitigations; P1 if sustained and breaches contractual latency SLO or blocks core workflow.

B) Escalation: Engage SRE (non-incident) + Dedicated runbook owner.
- Page SRE if throughput collapse or sustained queueing (P0/P1 characteristics).
- Otherwise: follow diagnostic runbook; schedule active monitoring during peak window.

C) First customer message (example):
“We’re seeing the peak-hour latency pattern you described and will investigate capacity/queueing signals on your Dedicated pool. We’ll review scheduler queue depth, GPU utilization, and batch/kv-cache behavior during the 10–12 window. Next update by <time>; in the interim, reducing max_tokens and enabling controlled retries can help limit tail latency.”

D) Missing fields:
- Workload characteristics during peak (prompt lengths, max_tokens distribution)
- Concurrency changes
- Whether routing/fallback policies are enabled

E) Known issue + mitigation:
- Confluence: Dedicated capacity latency spikes / noisy neighbor
- Safe mitigations: tune autoscaling thresholds; adjust max batch tokens; consider isolation settings; enable routing/fallback to secondary region/model variant (if contract allows).

Related example: Jira SUP-4924; runbook refresh: Linear ENG-2845

Slide 26 — Answer key: Scenario 4 (Private SSO/SAML failures)
A) Severity: P0 (Critical)
Rationale: total lockout; private enterprise; security/auth system.

B) Escalation: Immediate escalation to Private Deployments + Security escalation owner; involve SRE if platform auth components are implicated.
- Create restricted incident-style coordination thread if needed (do not paste sensitive IdP metadata broadly).

C) First customer message (example):
“We’re treating this as a critical access issue and have engaged our Private Deployments and Security teams. Please share the timestamp of the IdP change, the IdP metadata/certificate fingerprint (via the secure channel), and any error codes you see. Next update by <time>; we’ll prioritize a safe recovery path while protecting your account security.”

D) Missing fields:
- Exact IdP change details, metadata, certificate fingerprint, assertion settings
- Whether any break-glass admin account exists (per their setup)
- Private deployment version + recent config changes

E) Known issue + mitigation:
- Not always a “known issue.” Use internal Private SSO checklist/runbook.
- Important note: “emergency bypass” is not promised; any bypass must follow Security policy.

Related example: Jira SUP-4923

Slide 27 — Answer key: Scenario 5 (5xx in eu-west on pinned model version)
A) Severity: P1 (High) if sustained; P0 if effectively down and no workaround.

B) Escalation: Page SRE if signals indicate regional degradation; likely incident if multiple customers affected or core infrastructure.
- Also engage Runtime/Serving if model-version specific regression.

C) First customer message (example):
“We’re investigating elevated 5xx errors for model version v2026-02-10 in eu-west. We’ve engaged our on-call reliability team to assess regional/model health and will update you by <time>. If you’re able, a temporary failover to us-east or switching to the latest compatible model version may mitigate impact; we can help validate an option that aligns with your residency constraints.”

D) Missing fields:
- Confirmation of data residency requirements and whether failover is permitted
- Exact endpoints used + request pattern
- Any recent changes (customer deploy, request rate)

E) Known issue + mitigation:
- If a known issue exists for that model version/region: reference it.
- Safe mitigations: region failover hints (if allowed), model pin rollback/unpin guidance, reduced concurrency and retries with backoff.

Related example: Jira SUP-4925

Slide 28 — Tools/process updates you need to use starting now
- Jira fields/template updates (INT-1337): escalation required fields + SLA due dates
- Macro/snippet library (INT-1338): comms templates + restricted handling reminders
- Incident-bot workflow (GitHub incident-bot/pr_214): auto prompts for required fields + thread stub

If you’re not seeing fields/macros yet: post in #support-ops and tag Owen Phillips.

Slide 29 — Rollout checklist (for Support leads)
Within 1 week:
- Everyone completes this training (or watches recording)
- Pin Confluence playbook links in #support
- Update saved replies / macros to v2 templates
- Confirm oncall paging rules + backup contacts

Within 2–4 weeks:
- Review top 10 escalations for “required fields compliance”
- Update Known Issues pages where we keep giving custom advice
- Feedback loop to SRE on false pages (paging hygiene)

Slide 30 — FAQ (quick hits)
Q: If the customer is angry, can we page without required fields?
A: For P0/P1 we can page while collecting, but the first message to oncall must include (at minimum) tier, region, model, timestamps, and at least one request ID.

Q: Can we share internal dashboards with customers?
A: No. Summarize findings; use customer-safe language. Follow comms templates.

Q: Where do I put sensitive Private customer details?
A: Restricted channels/tickets only. Ask Security/Private Deployments if unsure.

Slide 31 — Appendix: Triage checklist (copy/paste)
1) Confirm tier + deployment mode
2) Time window + region + model/version
3) Error type: 5xx / 429 / timeout / streaming disconnect / auth
4) Request IDs + timestamps
5) Check Known Issues index
6) Provide validated workaround (if applicable)
7) Determine severity + escalation trigger
8) Send customer update with next update time

Slide 32 — Appendix: Customer update template (short)
“Thanks for your patience — we’re investigating <symptom> impacting <scope> in <region> for <model/version>. We’ve engaged <team> and are reviewing <what we’re checking>. Next update by <time>. In the meantime, <safe mitigation> may reduce impact; we can help you apply it.”

Slide 33 — Appendix: What not to say
- “This is definitely a platform bug.” (until confirmed)
- “We’ll have an RCA by tomorrow.” (unless committed by incident owner)
- “We can bypass auth/SSO quickly.” (security risk; not promised)
- “Just increase retries” (without backoff + retry budget guidance)

Slide 34 — Appendix: Where to send feedback
- Process/tooling issues: Jira INT-1337 / INT-1338
- Known Issues page gaps: ping Priya Shah + link ticket
- Paging hygiene / incident thresholds: ping Rafael Mendes or Tomáš Novák
- Docs wording: ping Elliot Price / Wei Chen / Kira Thompson

End of deck
